```text
domain:
    r: dim in [0, NR)          # outermost dimension: slices of A along r
    q: dim in [0, NQ)          # next outer: slices along q
    p: dim in [0, NP)          # output / contracted-dim index (C index p)
    s: dim in [0, NP)          # reduction index over the last dimension of A

data:
    # 3D tensor A[r,q,p], stored as A[r][q][p] in C (p fastest, then q, then r)
    # Linearization matches the Noarr layout scalar ^ p_vec ^ q_vec ^ r_vec.
    A[r, q, p]: inout num_t
        = (r, q, p) -> ((r * NQ) + q) * NP + p

    # 2D matrix C4[s,p], stored as C4[s][p] in C (p fastest, then s)
    # Matches scalar ^ p_vec ^ s_vec.
    C4[s, p]: in num_t
        = (s, p) -> s * NP + p

    # 1D temporary vector sum[p].
    # Semantically this is a scratch buffer private to each (r,q) slice:
    # in the original code it is reused for each (r,q) in sequence; under
    # parallelization it must be privatized (e.g. stack-allocated per worker).
    sum[p]: scratch num_t
        = (p) -> p

parameters:
    # Structural sizes are implied by the domains:
    #   NR, NQ, NP

    # Tunable constants for performance on the target machine.
    TP: int        # tile size for p (e.g., 32 or 64; must divide vector register usage well)
    TS: int        # tile size for s (e.g., 32 or 64; chosen to keep C4 tile in cache)
    VEC_P: int     # SIMD width along p (e.g., 8 for AVX2 float, 16 for AVX-512 float)
    UF_S: int      # unroll factor for inner s-loop to increase ILP
    T_PAR_RQ: int  # number of concurrent (r,q) tiles; used to bound sum[p] privatization
                   # so that extra memory for per-worker sum buffers < 50% of total

computation:
    # Baseline semantics, matching the C / Noarr kernel:
    # for (r)
    #   for (q) {
    #     for (p) {
    #       sum[p] = 0;
    #       for (s)
    #         sum[p] += A[r][q][s] * C4[s][p];
    #     }
    #     for (p)
    #       A[r][q][p] = sum[p];
    #   }
    #
    # We model this structure explicitly, then optimize it below.

    for r, q:
        # Zero the accumulation buffer for this (r,q) slice.
        for p:
            sum[p] = 0

        # Accumulate contributions over s into sum[p].
        # (This region will be transformed by interchange and blocking.)
        for p:
            for s:
                sum[p] += A[r, q, s] * C4[s, p]

        # Write the final result back into A.
        for p:
            A[r, q, p] = sum[p]

optimization:
    # 1. Exploit independence across (r,q) for coarse-grain parallelism.
    #    Each (r,q) slice only reads its own A[r,q,*] and writes back to it,
    #    and all use the read-only C4. No cross-(r,q) dependencies exist.
    #    The scratch array sum[p] is privatized per worker (e.g., as a
    #    stack-allocated NP-element buffer), so parallel threads do not race.
    #
    #    Memory overhead from privatized sum is NP * (#workers - 1), which
    #    remains well below 50% of the total footprint for typical NR·NQ ≫ #workers.
    parallelize(r)
    parallelize(q)

    # 2. Interchange p and s in the accumulation region to improve reuse and locality.
    #
    #    Original accumulation (per (r,q)):
    #        for p:
    #            for s:
    #                sum[p] += A[r,q,s] * C4[s,p]
    #
    #    After interchange(p,s) in this region, we conceptually get:
    #        for s:
    #            let a_rqs = A[r,q,s]                   # loaded once per s
    #            for p:
    #                sum[p] += a_rqs * C4[s,p]
    #
    #    Benefits:
    #      - A[r,q,s] is now loaded once per s and reused across all p, instead
    #        of being reloaded NP times (once for each p) in the original order.
    #      - C4[s,p] and sum[p] are traversed with unit stride along p
    #        (already row-major with p fastest), improving cache and SIMD efficiency.
    interchange(p, s)

    # 3. Block (tile) p and s to improve cache behavior for C4 and sum.
    #
    #    After the interchange, the hot region becomes (per (r,q)):
    #        for s:
    #            a_rqs = A[r,q,s]
    #            for p:
    #                sum[p] += a_rqs * C4[s,p]
    #
    #    We tile it as:
    #        for S in blocks of s with size TS:
    #          for P in blocks of p with size TP:
    #            for s in S:
    #              a_rqs = A[r,q,s]
    #              for p in P:
    #                sum[p] += a_rqs * C4[s,p]
    #
    #    TS, TP are chosen so that:
    #      - The working set C4[S, P] and sum[P] fit in L1/L2.
    #      - The additional working set per thread (TS * TP elements of C4
    #        plus TP elements of sum) is small compared to the global A and C4.
    block(p, P, TP)
    block(s, S, TS)
    hoist(S)      # iterate s-tiles outside p-tiles
    hoist(P)      # p-tiles remain outer to inner p within the tile

    # 4. Vectorize the innermost p-loop within tiles.
    #
    #    Inside each (S,P) tile, the innermost loop runs over consecutive p.
    #    Both C4[s,p] and sum[p] are contiguous in p, so we can safely
    #    vectorize along p with width VEC_P (e.g., 8 or 16 floats).
    vectorize(p, VEC_P)

    # 5. Unroll the s-loop within tiles to increase instruction-level parallelism
    #    and better hide latency of loads from A[r,q,s].
    unroll(s, UF_S)

    # 6. Layout considerations:
    #    - Keep A in row-major form with p as the innermost dimension:
    #          A[r,q,p] -> ((r * NQ) + q) * NP + p
    #      With the transformed loop nest, accesses to A[r,q,s] are
    #      performed in increasing s and thus still unit-stride.
    #    - Keep C4 in row-major form C4[s,p], as originally:
    #          C4[s,p] -> s * NP + p
    #      After the interchange, p is the innermost loop, so C4[s,p]
    #      is read sequentially along rows, which is optimal.
    #    - sum[p] remains a 1D contiguous buffer. With tiling over p,
    #      only a TP-sized window of sum is hot in cache at a time.
```

```text
domain:
    r: dim in [0, NR)          # outermost dimension in A, independent across iterations
    q: dim in [0, NQ)          # second dimension in A, also independent across iterations
    s: dim in [0, NP)          # reduction index (originally shares size with p)
    p: dim in [0, NP)          # output index

data:
    # 3D array A corresponding to C array A[NR][NQ][NP] accessed as A[r][q][p]
    # Row-major layout: p is the fastest-varying index in memory.
    A[r, q, p]: inout DATA_TYPE =
        (r, q, p) -> ((r * NQ) + q) * NP + p

    # 2D array C4 corresponding to C array C4[NP][NP] accessed as C4[s][p]
    # Row-major layout: p is the fastest-varying index in memory.
    C4[s, p]: in DATA_TYPE =
        (s, p) -> s * NP + p

    # Temporary vector used per (r, q) pair.
    # In the original code this is a global 1D array "sum[p]" reused for every (r, q);
    # here we model it as a per-(r, q) scratchpad without changing semantics.
    sum[p]: local DATA_TYPE =
        (p) -> p

parameters:
    # Tuning parameters for blocking and vectorization (chosen for x64 with sizeable caches).
    TR: int   # tile size in r (e.g., 8 or 16)
    TQ: int   # tile size in q (e.g., 8 or 16)
    TS: int   # tile size in s (e.g., 32 or 64)
    TP: int   # tile size in p for cache/SIMD (e.g., 32 or 64)
    VP: int   # SIMD width along p (e.g., 8 doubles or 16 floats on AVX-512)
    US: int   # unroll factor for the inner reduction over s (e.g., 2–8)

computation:
    # Mathematical semantics of the kernel:
    # For each (r, q), the NP-length row A[r, q, *] is multiplied by the NP×NP
    # matrix C4, producing a new row A'[r, q, *].
    #
    # A'[r, q, p] = sum over s of A[r, q, s] * C4[s, p]
    #
    # This is equivalent to the original code, which performs:
    #   for r, q:
    #     for p: sum[p] = 0
    #     for s:
    #       for p: sum[p] += A[r, q, s] * C4[s, p]
    #     for p: A[r, q, p] = sum[p]
    #
    # but expressed directly as a reduction.
    for r, q, p:
        A[r, q, p] = sum(s, A[r, q, s] * C4[s, p])

optimization:
    # High-level goal:
    #  - Exploit that (r, q) tiles are independent -> outer parallelism.
    #  - Exploit that for fixed (r, q, s) the value A[r, q, s] is reused across all p.
    #  - Traverse C4 row-major (s outer, p inner) to use contiguous accesses.
    #  - Keep partial sums in registers/L1 and write back to A only once.
    #  - Block loops in r, q, s, p to fit caches and improve TLB behavior.
    #  - Vectorize the innermost p-loop.

    # 1. Block outer spatial dimensions r and q for coarse-grain parallelism and cache reuse.
    block(r, R, TR)   # r = R * TR + r_in_tile, tiles in r of height TR
    block(q, Q, TQ)   # q = Q * TQ + q_in_tile, tiles in q of width TQ

    # Process tiles of (r, q) in any order; each tile is independent.
    parallelize(R)    # distribute R-tiles across cores
    parallelize(Q)    # optionally parallelize Q within each R-tile (nested or dynamic scheduling)

    # 2. Within each (R, Q) tile, use the more cache-friendly loop structure:
    #
    #   for each (r, q) in the tile:
    #     for p: sum[p] = 0
    #     for s:
    #       a = A[r, q, s]                 # load once per s
    #       for p: sum[p] += a * C4[s, p]  # reuse a across all p
    #     for p: A[r, q, p] = sum[p]
    #
    # Compared to the original Noarr implementation (which loops p outer, s inner),
    # this hoists the reduction index s outside p, reducing reloads of A[r, q, s]
    # by a factor of NP, while preserving the mathematical result.

    hoist(s)   # ensure the reduction loop over s is outer to the loop over p

    # 3. Tile both the output dimension p and the reduction dimension s.
    #
    # This controls working-set size:
    #  - Blocking p keeps a contiguous chunk of sum[p] and the corresponding
    #    C4[s, p] segment in L1/L2.
    #  - Blocking s limits the number of C4 rows processed before reusing sum[p].
    #
    # Effective computation inside a (R, Q) tile becomes:
    #
    #   for each (r, q) in tile:
    #     for each p-tile P:
    #       for p in P: sum[p] = 0
    #     for each s-tile S:
    #       for s in S:
    #         a = A[r, q, s]
    #         for each p-tile P:
    #           for p in P: sum[p] += a * C4[s, p]
    #     for each p-tile P:
    #       for p in P: A[r, q, p] = sum[p]
    #
    # Only the existing "sum[p]" buffer is used; no additional NP-sized arrays
    # are introduced, so extra memory is negligible.

    block(p, P, TP)   # introduce tile index P for p, with tile size TP
    block(s, S, TS)   # introduce tile index S for s, with tile size TS

    hoist(S)          # iterate s-tiles outside p-tiles to maximize reuse of A[r, q, s]

    # 4. Vectorize the innermost p-loop and unroll the s-loop.
    #
    # For each fixed (r, q, S, P), the inner-most work is:
    #   for s in S:
    #     a = A[r, q, s]
    #     for p in P: sum[p] += a * C4[s, p]
    #
    # This has a perfectly contiguous p dimension in memory, ideal for SIMD.
    # We use:
    #   - vectorize(p, VP): map p in P to SIMD lanes (e.g., 8 doubles per vector).
    #   - unroll(s, US): unroll the reduction loop to reduce loop overhead and
    #     expose instruction-level parallelism.

    vectorize(p, VP)  # SIMD across contiguous p within each P-tile
    unroll(s, US)     # unroll the inner reduction over s within each S-tile

    # 5. Arithmetic and memory optimizations (conceptual, not new loops):
    #
    #  - For each (r, q, s), hoist the load:
    #       a = A[r, q, s]
    #     and reuse it across all p in the current P-tile, avoiding redundant
    #     loads of A[r, q, s] present in the original Noarr loop structure.
    #
    #  - Maintain sum[p] in registers or L1 within each p-tile and only write
    #    back to A[r, q, p] once per p (after all s-tiles are accumulated).
    #
    #  - Implement the accumulation as fused multiply-add where available:
    #       sum[p] = fma(a, C4[s, p], sum[p])
    #    to reduce rounding error and improve throughput.
    #
    #  - Since (r, q) tiles never share A rows, C4 is read-only, and sum is
    #    per-(r, q), there are no cross-tile dependencies; only the reduction
    #    along s is ordered, which is preserved inside each (r, q, p) point.
```

```text
domain:
    # Problem dimensions (from defines.hpp / doitgen.hpp)
    r: dim in [0, NR)        # row index of A
    q: dim in [0, NQ)        # column index of A (second dimension)
    p: dim in [0, NP)        # output index and C4 column index
    s: dim in [0, NP)        # reduction index and C4 row index

data:
    # 3D tensor A, updated in-place.
    # Matches C layout A[r][q][p] with p as the fastest-varying index:
    #   offset_A(r,q,p) = ((r * NQ) + q) * NP + p
    A[r, q, p]: inout DATA_TYPE
        = (r, q, p) -> ((r * NQ) + q) * NP + p

    # Constant NP×NP transform matrix C4[s][p], row-major with p fastest:
    #   offset_C4(s,p) = s * NP + p
    C4[s, p]: in DATA_TYPE
        = (s, p) -> s * NP + p

    # Conceptual temporary: a private accumulation vector per (r, q, p).
    # In the original code this is a 1D array sum[p] reused for each (r, q).
    # We model it as sum_priv[r,q,p] to expose parallelism and independence.
    sum_priv[r, q, p]: local DATA_TYPE

parameters:
    # Tuning parameters (compile-time or runtime constants)
    TP: int > 0    # tile size along p (output index), e.g., 32 or 64
    TS: int > 0    # tile size along s (reduction index), e.g., 32 or 64
    VEC: int > 0   # SIMD vector width or its multiple, e.g., 8 or 16

computation:
    # Semantics: for each (r, q), compute
    #   A[r,q,p] := Σ_{s=0}^{NP-1} A_old[r,q,s] * C4[s,p]
    # where A_old is the value of A before the kernel.
    #
    # We logically separate three phases per (r, q):
    #   1. Initialize sum_priv[r,q,:] to 0
    #   2. Accumulate over s into sum_priv[r,q,:]
    #   3. Write back A[r,q,:] from sum_priv[r,q,:]

    for r, q:                               # all (r,q) planes are independent
        init_sum:
            for p in [0, NP):               # sum_priv[r,q,p] = 0 for all p
                sum_priv[r, q, p] = 0

        reduce:                             # matrix–vector-like multiplication
            # NOTE: This loop order (s outer, p inner) preserves the
            # per-element accumulation order over s compared to the original
            # kernel, so floating-point results are bitwise identical.
            for s in [0, NP):
                let a_rqs = A[r, q, s]      # A[r][q][s], contiguous in memory
                for p in [0, NP):           # C4[s,p] row, contiguous in memory
                    # sum_priv[r,q,p] += A[r,q,s] * C4[s,p]
                    sum_priv[r, q, p] = sum_priv[r, q, p] + a_rqs * C4[s, p]

        write_back:
            for p in [0, NP):
                A[r, q, p] = sum_priv[r, q, p]

dependencies:
    # For each (r, q, p), write_back must see the fully reduced sum over s.
    for r in [0, NR), q in [0, NQ), p in [0, NP):
        reduce(r, q, p) -> write_back(r, q, p)

optimization:
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 1. Parallelism over (r, q)
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Each (r, q) plane:
    #   - reads only A[r,q,*] and C4[* ,*]
    #   - writes only A[r,q,*] and sum_priv[r,q,*]
    # There are no cross-(r,q) dependencies, so we can execute (r, q)
    # iterations in parallel. In the actual implementation, this corresponds
    # to making the outer loops parallel (e.g., OpenMP parallel for over a
    # collapsed (r,q) space or a 2D partition).

    parallelize(r)
    parallelize(q)

    # Implementation note:
    #   sum_priv[r,q,*] is realized as a *thread-private* buffer sum[p] of
    #   length NP, reused across all (r,q) handled by that thread.
    #   - In purely sequential code: a single sum[NP] as in the original.
    #   - Under parallelize(r) / parallelize(q): each worker has its own
    #     private sum[NP], avoiding races and false sharing.
    #   The extra memory per thread is O(NP), negligible compared to
    #   A[NR][NQ][NP] + C4[NP][NP], and far below a 50% footprint increase.

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2. Blocking (tiling) in (s, p) for cache locality
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # For a fixed (r, q) we conceptually perform:
    #    sum_priv[r,q,:] += A[r,q,:]^T * C4[:,:]
    #
    # With s outer and p inner, we see:
    #    - A[r,q,s]  : contiguous in s (3rd dim of A, p/s fastest)
    #    - C4[s,p]   : contiguous in p (row-major)
    # Tiling s and p allows us to keep the active C4 sub-block and part of
    # sum_priv in L1/L2 cache, improving reuse and reducing bandwidth.

    block(s, S, TS)   # S indexes tiles of the reduction dimension s
    block(p, P, TP)   # P indexes tiles of the output dimension p

    # After blocking, the inner structure inside (r, q) becomes (schematically):
    #
    #   for S in [0, NP/TS):
    #     for s in tile_S(S):           # size TS
    #       a_rqs = A[r,q,s]
    #       for P in [0, NP/TP):
    #         for p in tile_P(P):       # size TP
    #           sum_priv[r,q,p] += a_rqs * C4[s,p]
    #
    # For any fixed p, the contributions are still accumulated in order s=0..NP-1,
    # because s is not reordered across tiles; only grouped.

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 3. Loop hoisting (scheduling outer loops)
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # We want the outer-most order to be:
    #   r -> q -> S -> P -> s -> p
    # so that:
    #   - (r, q) tiles are distributed across threads
    #   - Within each (r,q) tile we iterate S, then P
    #   - The innermost loop over p has unit stride and good locality.
    #
    # hoist(D) moves DIMENSION D as far out as legal; we hoist:
    #   - r and q over (s, p) to preserve independent planes
    #   - S and P over (s, p) to keep tile loops outside the fine-grain loops

    hoist(r)
    hoist(q)
    hoist(S)
    hoist(P)

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 4. SIMD vectorization and unrolling over p
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # In the innermost loops we have:
    #    sum_priv[r,q,p] += a_rqs * C4[s,p]
    # with p varying fastest:
    #    - access to sum_priv[r,q,p] is contiguous in p
    #    - access to C4[s,p] is contiguous in p
    # This is ideal for SIMD. We vectorize and unroll the p-loop.
    #
    # VEC is a tuning parameter, typically chosen as:
    #   - 8 for AVX2 doubles, 16 for AVX2 floats
    #   - 8 or 16 for AVX-512, depending on type and desired unroll
    # The compiler can map this to appropriate intrinsics.

    vectorize(p, VEC)
    unroll(p, VEC)

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 5. Arithmetic optimizations (implicit)
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # - The reordering from (original):
    #       for p: sum[p] = 0; for s: sum[p] += ...
    #   to (optimized):
    #       sum[:] = 0; for s: for p: sum[p] += ...
    #   does not change the *per-element* accumulation order over s, so
    #   floating-point results remain bitwise identical.
    # - Temporaries:
    #       let a_rqs = A[r,q,s]
    #   avoid repeated loads of A[r,q,s] inside the p-loop, reducing memory
    #   traffic and enabling more effective register allocation.
```

```text
domain:
    r: dim in [0, NR)
    q: dim in [0, NQ)
    p: dim in [0, NP)
    s: dim in [0, NP)

data:
    # A is updated in place; we model separate read/write views that alias the same storage.
    # Layout matches A_layout = p_vec ^ q_vec ^ r_vec with p the fastest-varying index.
    A_in[r, q, s]: in    num_t = (r, q, s) -> ((r * NQ) + q) * NP + s
    A[r, q, p]:   inout num_t = (r, q, p) -> ((r * NQ) + q) * NP + p

    # C4[s][p] with p the fastest-varying index (C4_layout = p_vec ^ s_vec).
    C4[s, p]: in num_t = (s, p) -> s * NP + p

    # Temporary 1D scratch buffer reused for each (r, q); logically private per worker/tile.
    sum_scratch[p]: local num_t = p  # contiguous 1D buffer of length NP

parameters:
    # Tunable blocking and vectorization parameters for the target machine.
    BR: int  # tile size for r
    BQ: int  # tile size for q
    BP: int  # tile size for p
    BS: int  # tile size for s
    VP: int  # SIMD width used when vectorizing along p

computation:
    # High-level mathematical specification:
    # For every (r, q, p),
    #   A[r, q, p] = Σ_s A_in[r, q, s] * C4[s, p]
    # A_in and A conceptually share the same storage; A_in is the read-only view.
    for r, q, p:
        A[r, q, p] = sum(s in [0, NP), A_in[r, q, s] * C4[s, p])

dependencies:
    # Each (r, q) slice is independent when it has its own sum_scratch buffer.
    # There are no flow, anti-, or output-dependencies between different (r, q) pairs.
    for r in [0, NR), q in [0, NQ):
        # compute_row(r, q) computes all A[r, q, *]
        compute_row(r, q) -> A[r, q, *]
    # For all (r, q) ≠ (r', q'), compute_row(r, q) is independent of compute_row(r', q').

optimization:
    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 0. In-place implementation with scratch buffer
    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # scratch(DATA, scope=(i1, i2, ...)) means DATA is logically private for
    # each combination of indices in scope. Here, each (r, q) (or each (R, Q)
    # tile after blocking) uses its own sum_scratch[p], implemented as a stack
    # or thread-private buffer. This keeps additional memory well below +50%.
    scratch(sum_scratch, scope=(r, q))

    # The corresponding structured implementation is:
    #   for r, q:
    #     for p: sum_scratch[p] = 0
    #     for s:
    #       a_rqs = A_in[r, q, s]
    #       for p:
    #         sum_scratch[p] += a_rqs * C4[s, p]
    #     for p:
    #       A[r, q, p] = sum_scratch[p]
    # This is algebraically equivalent to the high-level computation above.

    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 1. Outer parallelism and cache-friendly tiling over (r, q)
    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Block r and q to form coarse tiles that map naturally to cores.
    block(r, R, BR)          # r = R * BR + r_in,   0 ≤ r_in < BR
    block(q, Q, BQ)          # q = Q * BQ + q_in,   0 ≤ q_in < BQ

    # Hoist the tile loops outermost and parallelize across R-tiles.
    hoist(R)                 # outer loop over r-tiles
    hoist(Q)                 # next loop over q-tiles
    parallelize(R)           # distribute R-tiles across threads (e.g., OpenMP/TBB)
    # Optionally also parallelize(Q) when NR is small and NQ is large.

    # sum_scratch is privatized per (R, Q) tile (via scratch above), so there
    # are no data races between threads.

    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2. Locality and vectorization in the (p, s) sub-kernel
    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Within a fixed (R, Q, r_in, q_in) tile, we operate on the NP×NP
    # micro-kernel that computes:
    #   sum_scratch[p] = Σ_s A_in[r, q, s] * C4[s, p]
    # Use 2D blocking on (s, p) so each S×P tile of C4 and the corresponding
    # slice of sum_scratch fit in L1/L2 cache.
    block(s, S, BS)          # s = S * BS + s_in
    block(p, P, BP)          # p = P * BP + p_in

    # Traverse tiles in S-major, then P-major order; within each tile the
    # innermost loops use p_in for unit-stride memory accesses.
    hoist(S)
    hoist(P)

    # Inside each (S, P) tile we use the structure:
    #   for s_in:
    #     a_rqs = A_in[r, q, s]             # s is contiguous in A
    #     for p_in:
    #       # p is contiguous in C4 and in sum_scratch
    #       sum_scratch[p] += a_rqs * C4[s, p]

    # Exploit SIMD along the innermost p_in loop.
    vectorize(P, VP)         # operate on VP consecutive p indices at once

    # Optionally unroll the small reduction over s_in to increase ILP.
    #unroll(S, US)           # where US divides BS

    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 3. Data-layout rationale
    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # The loop order above is chosen to align with the physical layouts:
    #
    #   - A_in[r, q, s] has s as the fastest-varying index for each (r, q),
    #     so scanning s is unit-stride in memory.
    #
    #   - C4[s, p] is stored with p as the fastest-varying index, so scanning
    #     p in the innermost loop is unit-stride in memory.
    #
    # With the chosen blocking (S, P) and loop order (outer S, inner P, inner
    # p_in), both A_in and C4 are accessed with good spatial locality and the
    # scalar a_rqs avoids reloading A_in[r, q, s] for each p. No physical
    # re-layout of the arrays is required; all gains come from loop
    # reorganization, blocking, privatization of sum_scratch, and SIMD.
```

```text
domain:
    r: dim in [0, NR)          # row index of A
    q: dim in [0, NQ)          # column index of A (second dimension)
    s: dim in [0, NP)          # "source" index in the transform
    p: dim in [0, NP)          # "target" index in the transform

data:
    # 3D array A[r, q, p], row-major with p as the fastest-varying index.
    # Matches the C layout A[NR][NQ][NP] where A[r][q][p] is at:
    #   offset = ((r * NQ) + q) * NP + p
    A[r, q, p]: inout num_t = (r, q, p) -> ((r * NQ + q) * NP + p)

    # 2D transform matrix C4[s, p], row-major with p fastest.
    # Matches the C layout C4[NP][NP] where C4[s][p] is at:
    #   offset = s * NP + p
    C4[s, p]: in num_t = (s, p) -> (s * NP + p)

    # 1D temporary buffer sum[p], reused for each (r, q) plane.
    # Only one instance is needed at a time; when parallelizing across (r, q),
    # this buffer is made thread-private.
    sum[p]: tmp num_t = (p) -> p

parameters:
    # Problem sizes (already fixed by defines.hpp / doitgen.hpp in code).
    NR: int > 0
    NQ: int > 0
    NP: int > 0

    # Tuning parameters for blocking / vectorization on the target CPU.
    T_R: int > 0    # tile size in r  (e.g., 2–8 to fit per-thread working set in L2)
    T_Q: int > 0    # tile size in q  (e.g., 2–8)
    T_S: int > 0    # tile size in s  (e.g., 32–64)
    T_P: int > 0    # tile size in p  (e.g., 32–128, chosen w.r.t. SIMD width and cache)
    V_P: int > 0    # SIMD vector width along p (e.g., 8 doubles or 16 floats)
    U_P: int > 0    # unroll factor for the inner p-loop (typically a small multiple of V_P)

computation:
    # For each (r, q) plane of A, apply the same NP×NP transform C4 along the last
    # dimension. This is the mathematical operation:
    #
    #   A[r, q, p] ← sum_{s=0..NP-1} A[r, q, s] * C4[s, p]
    #
    # implemented via a reusable 1D buffer sum[p]. The loop ordering below is
    # already optimized compared to the naive code: we move the s-loop outside
    # the p-loop to reuse A[r, q, s] across all p, and to traverse C4 row-wise.

    for r, q:
        # 1. Initialize accumulation buffer for this (r, q):
        for p:
            INIT_SUM: sum[p] = 0

        # 2. Accumulate contributions from all s into sum[p].
        #    We hoist A[r, q, s] into a scalar a_rqs so it is loaded once and
        #    reused across all p, instead of being reloaded NP times.
        for s:
            let a_rqs = A[r, q, s]
            for p:
                ACCUM_SUM: sum[p] += a_rqs * C4[s, p]

        # 3. Write back the transformed row into A.
        for p:
            STORE_A: A[r, q, p] = sum[p]

dependencies:
    # For each fixed (r, q, p), the initialization must happen before any
    # accumulation, and all accumulations for that (r, q, p) must be complete
    # before the final store. Different (r, q) planes are independent.
    for r in [0, NR), q in [0, NQ), p in [0, NP), s in [0, NP):
        INIT_SUM(r, q, p) -> ACCUM_SUM(r, q, s, p)
        ACCUM_SUM(r, q, s, p) -> STORE_A(r, q, p)

optimization:
    # High-level algorithmic optimization (already reflected in the computation):
    #
    #   - Original kernel (in the provided code) conceptually does:
    #        for r, q:
    #          for p:
    #            sum[p] = 0
    #            for s:
    #              sum[p] += A[r, q, s] * C4[s, p]
    #          for p:
    #            A[r, q, p] = sum[p]
    #
    #     Each A[r, q, s] is reloaded NP times (once per p), and C4[s, p] is
    #     accessed with a large stride in memory.
    #
    #   - The model above uses a "plane-wise" accumulation order:
    #        for r, q:
    #          for p:          sum[p] = 0
    #          for s:
    #            a_rqs = A[r, q, s]
    #            for p:        sum[p] += a_rqs * C4[s, p]
    #          for p:          A[r, q, p] = sum[p]
    #
    #     This:
    #       * loads A[r, q, s] once and reuses it across all p,
    #       * walks C4[s, p] row-wise with p as the innermost index (contiguous),
    #       * keeps writes to A[r, q, p] contiguous in p.
    #     Thus, it drastically reduces memory traffic on A and improves
    #     locality for both C4 and A.

    # 1) Parallelize across independent (r, q) planes.
    #
    #    All computations for different (r, q) pairs are independent once sum[p]
    #    is made thread-private. We therefore:
    #
    #      - tile r and q to form coarse-grain work units (R, Q),
    #      - hoist these tiles to the outermost loops,
    #      - parallelize over R (and implicitly over Q inside each thread).
    #
    #    sum[p] is **privatized per parallel worker** (stack or thread-local
    #    allocation), which is feasible because it has size O(NP) << O(NR*NQ*NP).
    block(r, R, T_R)
    block(q, Q, T_Q)
    hoist(R)              # outermost: tiles of r
    hoist(Q)              # next: tiles of q inside each tile of r
    parallelize(R)        # distribute (R, Q) tiles across threads; privatize sum[p]

    # 2) Tile and vectorize along p (fastest-varying dimension).
    #
    #    The innermost numeric work for each (r, q, s) is:
    #       for p: sum[p] += a_rqs * C4[s, p]
    #
    #    This is a SAXPY-like operation over contiguous segments of both sum[p]
    #    and C4[s, p], ideal for SIMD. We:
    #
    #      - tile p into P (coarse tiles) and inner p (fine index),
    #      - hoist P outside the s-loop so that we reuse sum[p] and C4 tiles
    #        in cache across s,
    #      - vectorize over the inner p dimension,
    #      - optionally unroll that dimension to reduce loop overhead.
    block(p, P, T_P)
    hoist(P)              # loop nest becomes: for r, q, P, (INIT/ACCUM/STORE over inner p)
    vectorize(p, V_P)     # map inner p-loop to SIMD lanes (aligned contiguous access)
    unroll(p, U_P)        # optional further unrolling for ILP; chosen as a small multiple of V_P

    # 3) Tile s for cache reuse of A and C4 rows.
    #
    #    For each (r, q), the working set during accumulation is:
    #      - one row A[r, q, *] of length NP,
    #      - multiple rows C4[s, *] and the buffer sum[*].
    #
    #    Tiling s keeps the active subset of C4[s, *] small and improves temporal
    #    locality as we repeatedly multiply the same A[r, q, s] by a contiguous
    #    block of C4[s, p] and update a contiguous block of sum[p].
    block(s, S, T_S)
    hoist(S)              # loop order inside (R, Q, P) tiles: for S, for s in S-tile

    # 4) Resulting preferred execution order (schematic, respecting dependencies):
    #
    #    for R in tiles of r (parallelized):
    #      for Q in tiles of q:
    #        for r in R-tile:
    #          for q in Q-tile:
    #            for P in tiles of p:
    #              # INIT: zero sum over inner p in this tile
    #              for p in P-tile (vectorized, unrolled):
    #                INIT_SUM: sum[p] = 0
    #
    #              # ACCUM: reduce over S and inner s, updating sum[p]
    #              for S in tiles of s:
    #                for s in S-tile:
    #                  let a_rqs = A[r, q, s]              # scalar reused across p
    #                  for p in P-tile (vectorized, unrolled):
    #                    ACCUM_SUM: sum[p] += a_rqs * C4[s, p]
    #
    #              # STORE: write back contiguous block of A[r, q, p]
    #              for p in P-tile (vectorized, unrolled):
    #                STORE_A: A[r, q, p] = sum[p]
    #
    #    This schedule:
    #      - preserves all dependencies in the original kernel,
    #      - reduces reloads of A[r, q, s] from O(NP^2) to O(NP) per (r, q),
    #      - makes all accesses to C4 and A along p streaming and SIMD-friendly,
    #      - exposes coarse-grained parallelism in r (and q) for multi-core CPUs,
    #      - keeps the extra memory usage within ≈ O(NP) per thread via
    #        a privatized sum[p], well below the 50% overhead budget.
```
